'''''Cicuta''''', commonly known as '''water hemlock''', is a [[genus]] of four species of highly [[poisonous plant]]s in the family [[Apiaceae]]. They are [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] plants which grow up to {{convert|2.5|m|ft|0|sp=us}} tall, having distinctive small green or white flowers arranged in an umbrella shape ([[umbel]]). Plants in this genus may also be referred to as '''cowbane''' or '''poison parsnip'''. ''Cicuta'' is native to [[temperate]] regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]], mainly [[North America]] and [[Europe]], typically growing in [[wet meadow]]s, along streambanks and other wet and marshy areas. In the United Kingdom it is frequently found along canals. These plants bear a close resemblance to other members in the family Apiaceae and may be confused with a number of edible or poisonous plants. The common name hemlock may also be confused with poison hemlock (''[[Conium maculatum]]''), or with the [[Hemlock tree]].

Water hemlock is considered one of the most toxic plants in North America and Europe, being highly poisonous to humans.<ref name="Schep"/> Three members of the genus contain a [[toxin]] named [[cicutoxin]] which causes [[central nervous system]] stimulatory effects including [[seizure]]s following ingestion. Medical treatment of poisoning may include the use of [[activated charcoal]] to decrease [[gastrointestinal]] absorption of the toxic principle along with supportive care including [[anticonvulsant]] drugs such as a [[benzodiazepine]]. High doses of anticonvulsant medicine are often required to halt seizure activity and further medical care including [[intubation]] and [[mechanical ventilation]] may be required.

==Description==
''Cicuta'' spp. are [[Biennial plant|biennial]] plants that are all similar in [[morphology (biology)|morphology]], growing up to a maximum of {{convert|2.5|m|ft|0|sp=us}} in height. The stem of the plant is branching, erect, smooth and hollow (except for partitions at the junction of the leaves and stem), sometimes being purple-striped, or [[mottled]] (typically only ''C. maculata'' has the purple stripes or spots). Attached to the base of the stem is a [[tuberous root]] with thickened [[rootstock]]s. The rootstocks are multichambered and contain a yellowish oily liquid which turns reddish brown on exposure to air and emits a characteristic smell of raw parsnip. The [[Phyllotaxis|alternate]] [[leaves]] are two or three [[pinnate]]ly compound and may reach {{convert|30|-|90|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length. The [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]] are [[lanceolate]], [[Crenate|serrate]], {{convert|5|-|10|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} in length, and sharply toothed. The plant flowers in spring or early summer; the flowers are small with green or white petals clustered in an umbrella shape ([[umbel]]) characteristic to this family; the umbel measures {{convert|5-10|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} across. The plants produce a cylindrical fruit which is {{convert|4-6|mm|in|abbr=on|frac=32}} in length.<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Kingsbury"/><ref name="Burrows">{{cite book |last=Burrows|first=George |author2=Tyrl, Ronald |title=Toxic plants of North America|publisher= Iowa State Press |location=Ames (IA) |year=2001 |pages=49–54 |isbn=0-8138-2266-1 }}</ref> The plant is spread primarily by seeds which are produced in large numbers and are small in size.<ref name="Kingsbury"/>

==Taxonomy==
The genus ''Cicuta'' is one of many genera in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Apiaceae]], which is in the order [[Apiales]]. Apiaceae is also known as Umbelliferae, and both of these family names are permitted to be used by the [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants]].<ref name="Schep"/> In Europe, ''Cicuta'' was not distinguished from the similar genus ''[[Conium]]'' before the year 1500. The first mention of the genus in the [[United States]] was in the eighteenth century.<ref name="Kingsbury"/> [[Carl Linnaeus]] formally described three species in 1753.<ref name="Linnaeus">{{cite book |last=Linnaeus|first=Carl |title=Species plantarum|location=Stockholm |year=1753|pages=255–56 |url=http://www.botanicus.org/title/b12069590|language=la }}</ref> The [[type species]] is ''Cicuta virosa''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Le Roy|first=Abrams |author2=Ferris, Roxana Stinchfield |title=An illustrated flora of the Pacific States: Washington, Oregon, and California|url=https://archive.org/details/illustratedflora03abra|publisher=Stanford University Press |location=Stanford, California |year=1951|page=[https://archive.org/details/illustratedflora03abra/page/237 237] |isbn=0-8047-0005-2}}</ref> The genus is now recognized to comprise four species:<ref name="Mulligan"/>

Other species names such as ''Cicuta bolanderi'', ''Cicuta californica'', and ''Cicuta curtissii'' are older names now recognized to be [[variety (botany)|varieties]] of the widespread, [[Morphology (biology)|morphologically]] variable ''Cicuta maculata''.<ref name="Burrows"/> ''Cicuta maculata'' is now recognized to have four varieties: var. ''maculata'', var. ''angustifolia'', var. ''victorinii'', and var. ''bolanderi''.<ref name="Mulligan">{{cite journal |author=Mulligan GA |title=The genus Cicuta in North America |journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |volume=58 |issue=16 |pages=1755–67 |date=August 1980 |doi=10.1139/b80-204}}</ref> [[Phylogenetics|Phylogenetic]] analysis using the [[primary structure|sequences]] of nuclear [[ribosomal DNA]] [[internal transcribed spacer]] (ITS) loci was not conclusive but seems to show that ''C. bulbifera'' and ''C. virosa'' are [[monophyletic]], while ''C. douglasii'' may not be. It was also suggested a specimen from California may warrant recognition as a distinct species.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Downie SR, Lee CS |title=Phylogenetic relationships within ''Cicuta'' (Apiaceae tribe Oenantheae) inferred from nuclear rDNA ITS and cpDNA sequence data |journal=Canadian Journal of Botany|volume=84 |issue=3 |pages=453–68 |date=March 2006|doi=10.1139/B06-016}}</ref> Other common names for the genus in general include poison parsnip, beaver poison, wild carrot, wild parsnip, and false parsley.<ref name="Landers"/>

==Similar species==
[[File:Cicuta virosa - Oslo Botanical Garden - IMG 8917.jpg|thumb|alt=Plant with green and red leaves |right|''[[Cicuta virosa]]'']]
Members of the family Apiaceae bear close resemblance to each other, and have many characteristics in common. ''Cicuta'' spp. are often mistaken for edible plants such as wild celery (''[[Angelica archangelica]]''), celery (''[[Apium graveolens]]''), pignut (''[[Conopodium majus]]''), wild carrot (''[[Daucus carota]]''), wild parsnip (''[[Pastinaca sativa]]''), and water parsnip (''[[Berula]]'' spp.).<ref name="Schep"/> One of the more common misidentifications is between water hemlock and water parsnip; both have clusters of small white flowers shaped like umbrellas, and both have the same habitat near the shoreline of lakes and rivers. Differences between water parsnip and water hemlock include the water parsnip having leaves only once [[Compound leaf|compound]] while the water hemlock has leaves which are two or three times compound. Water hemlock also has a large swelling at the stem base which water parsnip lacks. Additionally, water hemlock has [[bract]]s at the base of each small flower cluster, not at the base of the main flower head,<ref>{{cite web |title=Western Water Hemlock |publisher=Government of Saskatchewan |url=http://www.agriculture.gov.sk.ca/Default.aspx?DN=6896bcb3-d202-43e0-ace9-c4ec72d8835d |access-date=2008-08-03 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081008111353/http://www.agriculture.gov.sk.ca/Default.aspx?DN=6896bcb3-d202-43e0-ace9-c4ec72d8835d |archive-date=2008-10-08 }}</ref> while water parsnip has both bracts at the base of flowers and also at the main flower head.<ref>{{cite web |title=Water Parsnip |publisher=Government of Saskatchewan |url=http://www.agriculture.gov.sk.ca/Default.aspx?DN=e2b0945b-6609-4790-ae82-8fdd9135af26 |access-date=2008-08-03 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081008111400/http://www.agriculture.gov.sk.ca/Default.aspx?DN=e2b0945b-6609-4790-ae82-8fdd9135af26 |archive-date=2008-10-08 }}</ref>

Additionally, there can be confusion between the various water hemlock species and poison hemlock (''[[Conium maculatum]]'')<ref>{{cite journal |author=Hollman A |title=Points: Hemlock poisoning |journal=British Medical Journal (Clinical Research Ed.)|volume=296 |issue=6618 |page=361 |year=1988 |doi=10.1136/bmj.296.6618.361-h |pmc=2544856 }}</ref> as the common name hemlock is applied to both ''Cicuta'' and ''Conium maculatum''.<ref name="Schep2">{{cite journal |vauthors=Schep LJ, Slaughter RJ, Beasley DM |s2cid=28312730 |title=Nicotinic plant poisoning |journal=Clinical Toxicology |volume=47 |issue=8 |pages=771–81 |date=September–October 2009 |pmid=19778187 |doi=10.1080/15563650903252186 |issn=1556-3650}}</ref> Both are poisonous and can be differentiated by differences in their root structure. Water hemlock has a branched root systems with tubules, while poison hemlock has a single tap root.<ref name="Schep"/> Another reliable method to identify water hemlock is to examine the leaf veins. Water hemlock is unique in the family Apiaceae in that it has leaf veins which terminate in the notches between the leaf tips, rather than extend to the tip of the leaf, as is found in the leaf structure of other members of this family.<ref name="Kingsbury"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Cicuta'' spp. are found growing across North America and Europe. Typically, they grow in wet habitats usually alongside ponds and streams, in marshes or swamps, or areas that are swampy at least part of the year. Plants can also be found growing in water.<ref name="Kingsbury">{{cite book |last=Kingsbury |first=J.M. |title=Poisonous Plants of the United States and Canada |publisher=Prentice-Hall |year=1964 |edition=3 |location=Englewood Cliffs (NJ) |pages=[https://archive.org/details/poisonousplantso00king/page/373 373–79] |isbn=0-13-685016-2 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/poisonousplantso00king/page/373 }}</ref><ref name="Burrows"/> Of the four species, ''[[Cicuta maculata]]'' has the most widespread distribution occurring across the majority of North America. ''[[Cicuta bulbifera]]'' also has a relatively large distribution, found throughout Northern North America. ''[[Cicuta douglasii]]'' is found in the northwest corner of North America, while ''[[Cicuta virosa]]'' is found in central and northern [[Europe]] (including the [[British Isles]]), northern [[Eurasia]], and in the far north of North America.<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Burrows"/>

==Toxicity==
[[File:Cicutoxin.svg|thumb|right|alt=The chemical structure of cicutoxin, the toxin responsible for poisoning following ingestion of Cicuta plants |[[Cicutoxin]] is the major poison in ''Cicuta'' spp. plants.]]
All members of ''Cicuta'' contain high levels of the poisonous principle [[cicutoxin]], an [[Saturated and unsaturated compounds|unsaturated]] [[Aliphatic compound|aliphatic]] [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]] that is [[chemical structure|structurally]] closely related to the toxin [[oenanthotoxin]] found in the plant [[Oenanthe crocata|hemlock water dropwort]]. Cicutoxin is present at all stages of growth and in all parts of the plant, but is most concentrated in the roots which appear to be the most toxic in the early spring.<ref name="Schep"/> Its primary toxic effect is to act as a stimulant in the [[central nervous system]]. It is a non-competitive [[gamma-aminobutyric acid]] (GABA) [[receptor antagonist]]. Cicutoxin acts on the GABA<sub>A</sub> receptor causing a block of the [[chloride channel]] which results in [[neuronal depolarization]]. In the presence of cicutoxin, this depolarization continues unabated, causing cell overactivity. This hyperactivity in brain cells results in seizures.<ref name="Schep"/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Uwai K, Ohashi K, Takaya Y, Ohta T, Tadano T, Kisara K, Shibusawa K, Sakakibara R, Oshima Y |title=Exploring the structural basis of neurotoxicity in C(17)-polyacetylenes isolated from water hemlock |journal=Journal of Medicinal Chemistry |volume=43 |issue=23 |pages=4508–15 |date=November 2000 |pmid=11087575 |doi=10.1021/jm000185k |issn=0022-2623}}</ref> Cicutoxin is very poisonous, and water hemlock is considered one of North America's most toxic plants.<ref name="Schep">{{cite journal |vauthors=Schep LJ, Slaughter RJ, Becket G, Beasley DM |s2cid=21855822 |title=Poisoning due to water hemlock |journal=Clinical Toxicology |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=270–78 |date=April 2009 |pmid=19514873 |doi=10.1080/15563650902904332 |issn=1556-3650}}</ref><ref name="Mutter">{{cite journal |author=Mutter L |title=Poisoning by Western Water Hemlock |journal=Canadian Journal of Public Health|volume=67 |issue=5 |page=386 |date=September 1976 |pmid=991044 |issn=0008-4263}}</ref> Ingestion of ''Cicuta'' can be fatal in humans, and there are reports in medical literature of severe poisoning and death as early as 1670.<ref name="Schep"/> A number of people have also died following ingestion of the plant in the 20th and 21st century.<ref name="Landers">{{cite journal |vauthors=Landers D, Seppi K, Blauer W |title=Seizures and Death on a White River Float Trip: Report of Water Hemlock Poisoning |journal=The Western Journal of Medicine|volume=142 |issue=5 |pages=637–40 |date=May 1985 |pmid=4013278 |pmc=1306130 |issn=0093-0415 |format=Free full text}}</ref><ref name="CDC">{{cite journal |author=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) |title=Water hemlock poisoning--Maine, 1992 |journal=MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report |volume=43 |issue=13 |pages=229–31 |date=April 1994 |pmid=8145712 |issn=0149-2195 }}</ref><ref name="Heath">{{cite journal |author=Heath KB |title=A fatal case of apparent water hemlock poisoning |journal=Veterinary and Human Toxicology |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=35–6 |date=February 2001 |pmid=11205076 |issn=0145-6296 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Vogt E |title=[Water hemlock (''Cicuta virosa'') poisoning; report of two cases.] |language=no |journal=Tidsskrift for den Norske Lægeforening |volume=71 |issue=18 |pages=577–78 |date=September 1951 |pmid=14884156 |issn=0029-2001}}</ref><ref name="Withers">{{cite journal |doi=10.1056/NEJM196909042811029 |vauthors=Withers LM, Cole FR, Nelson RB |title=Water-hemlock poisoning |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=281 |issue=10 |pages=566–67 |date=September 1969 |pmid=5800524 |issn=0028-4793 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Litovitz TL, Bailey KM, Schmitz BF, Holm KC, Klein-Schwartz W |title=1990 annual report of the American Association of Poison Control Centers National Data Collection System |journal=The American Journal of Emergency Medicine |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=461–509 |date=September 1991 |pmid=1863304 |doi=10.1016/0735-6757(91)90216-7 |issn=0735-6757 }}</ref>

The {{LD50}} in mice administered cicutoxin by [[intraperitoneal injection]] is 48.3 milligrams per kilogram [[body weight]]; this compares with 5.9 mg/kg for mice given [[potassium cyanide]] by [[intraperitoneal injection]], while the LD<sub>50</sub> for [[arsenic]] via intraperitoneal injection in mice is 46.2 mg/kg.<ref>{{cite book |last=Lewis|first=Richard J |title=Sax's dangerous properties of industrial materials|url=https://archive.org/details/saxsdangerouspro0000lewi|url-access=registration|publisher=Van Nostrand Reinhold |location=New York |year=1996 |pages=270–1, 865, 2758|isbn=0-471-35407-4 }}</ref> The exact toxic dose of plant material in humans is unknown; it is thought ingestion of water hemlock in any quantity can result in poisoning, and very small amounts may lead to death.<ref name="Schep"/> Poisoning has been reported following children blowing whistles made from the hollow stem of water hemlock plants.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Miller MM |title=Water hemlock poisoning |journal=Journal of the American Medical Association |volume=101 |issue=11|pages=852–53 |year=1933|doi=10.1001/jama.1933.27430360001011}}</ref> Intoxication has also been reported following skin contact with the plant; in one case, a family of five rubbed the plant onto the skin and were poisoned, with two children dying.<ref name="Egdahl">{{cite journal |author=Egdahl A |title=A case of poisoning due to eating poison hemlock (''Cicuta maculata'') with a review of reported cases |journal=Archives of Internal Medicine |volume=7 |pages=348–56 |year=1911 |doi=10.1001/archinte.1911.00060030061002|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1423309 }}</ref> [[Livestock]] have long been the worst affected, leading to the common name "cowbane". Poisoning in livestock is common and typically occurs following ingestion of roots of the plant. When the ground is soft in Spring, grazing animals tend to pull the entire plant out of the ground, ingesting both the foliage and the roots. Roots exposed by ploughing can also be the source of livestock poisonings.<ref name="Kingsbury"/> Ingestion of plant material may cause death in the animal in as little as 15 minutes.<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=Water hemlock (''Cicuta douglasii'') |publisher= United States Department Of Agriculture |date=7 February 2006 |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/pacific-west-area/logan-ut/poisonous-plant-research/docs/water-hemlock-cicuta-douglasii/|access-date=13 June 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Panter KE, Keeler RF, Baker DC |title=Toxicoses in livestock from the hemlocks (''Conium'' and ''Cicuta'' spp.) |journal=Journal of Animal Science |volume=66 |issue=9 |pages=2407–13 |date=September 1988 |pmid=3049497 |issn=0021-8812 |url=http://jas.fass.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=3049497 |format=Free full text |doi=10.2527/jas1988.6692407x |url-access=subscription }}{{Dead link|date=July 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Smith RA, Lewis D |title=Cicuta toxicosis in cattle: case history and simplified analytical method |journal=Veterinary and Human Toxicology |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=240–41 |date=June 1987 |pmid=3604044 }}</ref>

===Symptoms===
Upon consumption, both in humans and other species, the symptoms of poisoning are characterized mainly by generalized [[seizures]].<ref name="Schep"/> The onset of symptoms following ingestion may be as soon as 15 minutes. Initial symptoms may include [[nausea]], [[vomiting]], [[abdominal pain]], [[tremor]]s, [[confusion]], weakness, [[dizziness]], and drowsiness,<ref name="Mutter"/><ref name="Stratton">{{cite journal |author=Stratton MR |title=Water hemlock poisoning|journal=Colorado Medicine |volume=16 |pages=104–11 |year=1919 }}</ref> although the rapid onset of seizure activity may be the first sign presented following poisoning. Seizures are usually described as [[clonic]] or [[tonic–clonic]].<ref name="Schep"/> Complications of ongoing seizure activity include [[hyperthermia|increased body temperature]], [[metabolic acidosis|decreases in the pH of the blood]] (metabolic acidosis), [[cerebral edema|swelling in the brain]], [[coagulopathy|blood coagulation disorders]], [[rhabdomyolysis|muscle breakdown]] (rhabdomyolysis), and [[kidney failure]].<ref name="Schep"/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Carlton BE, Tufts E, Girard DE |title=Water hemlock poisoning complicated by rhabdomyolysis and renal failure |journal=Clinical Toxicology|volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=87–92 |year=1979 |pmid=35306 |doi=10.3109/15563657909030117 |issn=0009-9309 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Short J |title=Water hemlock poisoning |journal=Emergency Nurse |volume=14 |issue=7 |pages=18–19 |date=November 2006 |pmid=17140092 |issn=1354-5752 |doi=10.7748/en2006.11.14.7.18.c4215}}</ref> Additional neurological symptoms may include [[hallucinations]], [[delirium]], [[paresthesia|tingling, pricking, or numbness of a person's skin]], [[mydriasis|dilated pupils]], and [[coma]].<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Mutter"/> [[Cardiovascular]] symptoms include alternating [[bradycardia|slow]] or [[tachycardia|fast heart rate]]<ref>{{cite journal |author=Gompertz LM |title=Poisoning with water hemlock (''Cicuta maculata''). Report of seventeen cases|journal=Journal of the American Medical Association |volume=87 |issue=16 |pages=1277–78 |year=1926 |doi=10.1001/jama.1926.02680160025008 }}</ref> and alternating [[hypotension|low]] and [[hypertension|high blood pressure]].<ref name="Costanza"/> Other cardiac effects may include [[ECG]] abnormalities such as widening of the [[PR interval]], [[supraventricular tachycardia]], and [[ventricular fibrillation]].<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="CDC"/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kass A, Pedersen H |title=[Water hemlock (cicutoxin) poisoning; review and personal observations.] |language=no |journal=Tidsskrift for den Norske Lægeforening |volume=71 |issue=18 |pages=579–80 |date=September 1951 |pmid=14884157 |issn=0029-2001}}</ref> Symptoms of excess [[salivation]], [[wheezing]], [[dyspnea|respiratory distress]], and [[apnea|absence of breathing]] have also been reported.<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Stratton"/>

Death is usually caused by [[respiratory failure]] or [[ventricular fibrillation]] secondary to ongoing seizure activity;<ref name="Schep"/> fatalities have occurred within a few hours of ingestion.<ref name="Burrows"/> Poisoned people who recover usually regain consciousness and seizures cease within 24 to 48 hours of poisoning, although seizures may persist for up to 96 hours.<ref name="Schep"/> There are occasional long-term effects, such as [[retrograde amnesia]] of the events leading to intoxication and the intoxication itself.<ref name="Landers"/><ref name="Stratton"/><ref name="Costanza">{{cite journal |vauthors=Costanza DJ, Hoversten VW |title=Accidental ingestion of water hemlock. Report of two patients with acute and chronic effects |journal=California Medicine|volume=119 |issue=2 |pages=78–82 |date=1 August 1973|pmid=4726956 |pmc=1455113 |issn=0008-1264}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Knutsen OH, Paszkowski P |title=New aspects in the treatment of water hemlock poisoning |journal=Journal of Toxicology. Clinical Toxicology |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=157–66 |year=1984 |pmid=6502788 |doi=10.3109/15563658408992551 |issn=0731-3810}}</ref> Other ongoing mild effects may include [[anxiety|restlessness]], [[muscle weakness]], [[Fasciculation|twitching]], and [[anxiety]].<ref name="Schep"/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Applefeld JJ, Caplan ES |title=A case of water hemlock poisoning |journal=Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians |volume=8 |issue=10 |pages=401–403 |date=October 1979 |pmid=491328 |doi=10.1016/S0361-1124(79)80404-9 |issn=0361-1124}}</ref> Complete resolution of symptoms may take a number of days, or these ongoing symptoms may persist for months after poisoning.<ref name="Schep"/>

===Diagnosis and treatment===
Water hemlock poisoning is usually diagnosed following a history of plant ingestion and symptoms of abrupt onset of seizures.<ref name="Heath"/><ref name="Starreveld"/> Laboratory tests to determine the presence of cicutoxin in the blood such as [[spectrofluorimetry]], [[high pressure liquid chromatography]], [[thin layer chromatography]], and [[mass spectrometry]] have been used to detect cicutoxin, but these tests are not performed routinely in [[Medical laboratory|hospital laboratories]].<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Froberg">{{cite journal |vauthors=Froberg B, Ibrahim D, Furbee RB |title=Plant poisoning |journal=Emergency Medicine Clinics of North America |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=375–433; abstract ix |date=May 2007 |pmid=17482026 |doi=10.1016/j.emc.2007.02.013}}</ref> If a sample of the plant ingested has been retained, diagnosis can be confirmed by having the plant identified by a botanist.<ref name="Schep"/>

Initial treatment of poisoning may include [[gastrointestinal]] decontamination with [[activated charcoal]].<ref name="Froberg"/> Decontamination is typically performed only if a potentially toxic amount of plant matter has been ingested up to one hour previously, and the patient has a normal intact [[airway]] or has been [[Intubation|intubated]].<ref name="Schep"/> There is no specific antidote for water hemlock poisoning, and treatment consists mainly of supportive care. Treatment may include control of [[seizure]]s with the administration of a [[benzodiazepine]] such as [[lorazepam]] or [[diazepam]], or, if seizures are refractory to this treatment, a [[barbiturate]] such as [[phenobarbital]] is administered.<ref name="Schep"/> The [[anticonvulsant]] [[phenytoin]] is not recommended, as it has not been shown to be effective for seizure control following water hemlock poisoning.<ref name="Starreveld">{{cite journal |vauthors=Starreveld E, Hope E |s2cid=39937321 |title=Cicutoxin poisoning (water hemlock) |journal=Neurology |volume=25 |issue=8 |pages=730–34 |date=August 1975 |pmid=1171406 |issn=0028-3878 |doi=10.1212/wnl.25.8.730}}</ref> Treatment with high doses of benzodiazepines or barbiturates may cause respiratory depression, and respiratory support including [[intubation]] and [[mechanical ventilation]] is required in these patients.<ref name="Schep"/> Continuous [[electroencephalography]] monitoring is recommended in symptomatic patients.<ref name="Schep"/>

Further treatment for complications of [[metabolic acidosis]], [[rhabdomyolysis]], [[hyperthermia]], or low blood pressure may be required. Metabolic acidosis is treated by administering [[sodium bicarbonate]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Ball MJ, Flather ML, Forfar JC |title=Hemlock water dropwort poisoning |journal=Postgraduate Medical Journal |volume=63 |issue=739 |pages=363–65 |date=May 1987 |pmid=3671269 |pmc=2428460 |doi=10.1136/pgmj.63.739.363 |issn=0032-5473 |format=Free full text }}</ref> Low blood pressure is usually treated with intravenous [[fluid replacement]], but the administration of [[dopamine]] or [[norepinephrine]] may be required to restore blood pressure.<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Froberg"/> The management of rhabdomyolysis includes ensuring adequate hydration and urinary alkalinization; a complication of rhabdomyolysis is [[acute kidney injury]], which may require management with [[hemodialysis]].<ref name="Schep"/> However, hemodialysis, [[hemoperfusion]], or other [[extracorporeal]] techniques do not remove cicutoxin from the blood and are therefore not useful in [[Poison#Enhanced excretion|enhancing elimination]].<ref name="Schep"/><ref name="Froberg"/>
